title: NOT Every Minute Matters
author: Wheeler
summary: A UK teacher reflects on the culture of performative busyness that has taken hold in schools, where a student sitting quietly after completing their work is treated as a crisis requiring immediate intervention. The author describes witnessing a senior leader cross a classroom to whisper to a teacher because a child was momentarily idle, fearing that observers from the trust might see it as evidence of poor instruction. This incident reveals how accountability structures have created layers of fear and surveillance that distort what effective teaching looks like, prioritizing the appearance of productivity over genuine learning. The article argues that moments of stillness, completion, and quiet thought are not failures but natural parts of the learning process. Students need space to finish a task, rest briefly, and process what they have done without every second being filled to satisfy observers. When teachers are compelled to maintain visible busyness at all times, they shift from educators into performers, and the children in their care lose something essential about what it feels like to simply be done.
points: Accountability cultures in schools have created pressure to eliminate visible student idle time, treating completion and brief rest as instructional failures
Layers of fear and surveillance between students, teachers, senior leaders, and trust inspectors distort authentic teaching into performance of busyness
Students need space to finish work and rest briefly without every second being optimized; not every minute needs to be visibly productive
quotes: Senior leaders in the room, and above them, people from the trust.
Partway through the lesson a pupil finished the task and sat there for a moment, done.
And one of the senior leaders actually crossed the room and whispered to her — embarrassed for her, worried on her behalf — because the trust people might notice a child briefly idle and be annoyed.
A child resting for a minute, having finished the work, was a threat to a teacher’s reputation — and a senior leader felt that so strongly it was worth interrupting the lesson to manage it.
If you teach you’ve had it said to you, probably in your training year, probably many times since.
A child sitting idle is a small emergency, and if someone walks in while it’s happening it’s your emergency.

That’s the thread running through everything I write — the phrases that get repeated at teachers until they feel like laws of nature, when nobody in the building can tell you where they came from or whether they’re true.
And this one collapses on contact with research nobody actually disputes.
